data: Launched Apollo 8, 9 and 11–17 (Apollo 9 in Earth orbit; Apollo 10 flew from 39B); today flies Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Crew Dragon

Operational pad at NASA Kennedy Space Center. Saturn V era 1967-1973 (Apollo 4 through Skylab); Shuttle era 1981-2011 (STS). Falcon 9 from 2017; Falcon Heavy from 2018. Coordinates and operational history from NASA KSC fact sheets and FAA registry.

Launch Complex 39A was built around an idea nearly as radical as the rocket it served: don't build the rocket at the pad. Instead, stack the Saturn V inside the cavernous Vehicle Assembly Building, then carry the whole ~3,000-tonne stack out to the pad — standing upright — on a crawler-transporter creeping along at walking pace. That "clean pad" approach let one site turn around the largest rocket ever flown far faster than assembling it in place ever could. The design outlived Apollo by half a century: the same pad launched most of the Space Shuttle fleet and, leased to SpaceX in 2014, now flies Falcon Heavy and astronauts on Crew Dragon. Good infrastructure, it turns out, is the quietest kind of moonshot — build it once and it keeps paying off.

Built for Saturn V, kept for the Shuttle, leased to SpaceX in 2014. From Pad A: Apollo 4 (the first Saturn V), Apollo 11 (the first lunar landing), Apollo 13, Apollo 17 (the last lunar landing), Skylab, eighty-two Space Shuttle flights including the first STS-1, and since 2017 every Falcon Heavy and every Crew Dragon to the ISS. The same flame trench, the same crawlerway, three eras of US human spaceflight.
First humans to leave low Earth orbit + orbit the Moon
First humans on another celestial body
First crewed LM flight — Earth-orbit LM separation + rendezvous tests
Second crewed Moon landing — pinpoint touchdown 163 m from Surveyor 3
The mission that turned a near-disaster into NASA's most celebrated rescue
Third lunar landing — Apollo 13's lost target reached; Shepard's golf shots
First J-mission — extended stay, first Lunar Roving Vehicle, "Genesis Rock"
Last crewed mission to the Moon (and the only Apollo with a trained geologist)
First Moon landing in the lunar highlands — Descartes; John Young's "lunar Grand Prix"
USA-277 — 780 days on orbit, KSC Shuttle Landing Facility
First all-civilian orbital spaceflight; raised $243M for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital
USA-358 / USSF-52 — 434 days on orbit, Vandenberg SFB
First commercial spacewalk; highest Earth orbit by humans since Apollo 17 (1408 km)
First crewed lunar lander; Eagle, Antares, Falcon...
USSF reusable robotic spaceplane — multi-year classified orbital missions, the only US spaceplane operational after the Shuttle's retirement
Apollo 10 + Skylab + 53 Shuttle flights; now NASA's SLS / Artemis pad
USAF Atlas-Centaur pad — Mariner 10, Pioneer 11 (1973), Pioneer Venus (1978); now Blue Origin New Glenn (leased 2015, flew 2025)
NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11
Australia's first satellite, WRESAT (1967), and Britain's Black Arrow launch of Prospero (1971)
Italian sea platform off Kenya that launched Uhuru, the first satellite dedicated to X-ray astronomy
Russia's northern military cosmodrome — more launches than any other site
